transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-12-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Eli Turner (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Aurelius Infra), Jamal Reed (Aurelius ML), Marta Alvarez (Aurelius Security), Noah Kim (Aurelius Platform)

[00:00] Eli: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick round of intros, then Samir will jump into the Private VPC networking and runtime considerations.
[00:18] Priya: Hi, Priya here, infra eng, focused on networking and infra constraints.
[00:22] Jamal: Jamal, ML eng, I'll be focused on throughput, kv cache behavior and latency.
[00:27] Marta: Marta, security, SOC2, KMS questions.
[00:30] Noah: Noah, platform, operations and cost.
[00:34] Samir: Great, I'll share my screen in a sec, walk through three patterns we see: PrivateLink control plane, VPC endpoint powered model-serving, and fully on-prem with direct connect. We'll call out networking gotchas and runtime impacts.
[01:02] Samir: First, PrivateLink (sometimes folks say Privatelink) gives you an interface endpoint so the control plane talk doesn't go over public internet, it's an ENI inside your subnet peered to our service. This avoids NAT egress for control plane calls.
[01:18] Priya: So control plane traffic would be internal, but what about telemetry/metrics? we want them on a private channel too.
[01:25] Samir: Yep, telemetry can flow via PrivateLink too; we push telemetry to our collector endpoint. If you want full isolation, you can route all outbound to a proxy in a protected subnet, or use a dedicated endpoint. Some customers put a proxy/forwarder in their mgmt VPC.
[01:45] Jamal: Quick question — runtime calls from our app to the model endpoints, will that also use PrivateLink? or is that only control plane?
[01:52] Samir: Good question. Two patterns: 1) control plane via PrivateLink and data plane uses VPC peering or private peering so inference traffic stays within your AZs; or 2) expose model-serving interface endpoints as AWS Interface Endpoints (we've seen customers use ENIs for the model nodes). Each has different scaling and IP limits.
[02:18] Priya: IP limits — we have a tight /20 per environment, worried about ENI exhaustion if we spawn many pods.
[02:25] Samir: Right — ENI/IP exhaustion is common. For high density we recommend placing runtime workers on instances with multiple IP addresses per ENI, or use AWS CNI with custom networking, or leverage AWS's secondary IPs. Alternatively, use an internal NLB + private link pattern so you don't need hundreds of interface endpoints.
[02:48] Noah: What's the tradeoff there on latency? adding a NAT/proxy or NLB layer adds ms. Our SLOs are 50-100ms p50 for single-turn responses.
[02:58] Samir: Typical numbers: colocated inference in same AZ, on good instances, p50 token latency can be single-digit ms per token for optimized runtimes; however cross-AZ hops, extra NAT or proxy layers, or cold KV cache misses can add 10s to 100s of ms. For your 50-100ms SLO, we'd prioritize same-AZ placement and avoid unnecessary NAT egress in the hot path.
[03:30] Jamal: About KV cache — how persistent is it across requests? if we have many short-lived containers, will the KV cache warmup blow our latency?
[03:40] Samir: KV cache (we sometimes see logs as K-V cash in transcripts) is kept in-process on the runtime node. For multi-turn chat you want sticky sessions or a shared cache layer. We offer options: 1) per-worker KV in-memory (fast), but needs session affinity; 2) a shared Redis-like KV in VPC for large scale, but that adds network RTT per cache hit. If you use shared KV over network you need sub-ms latency or you'll pay with token latency.
[04:12] Priya: If we use shared KV, does that require us to open additional security group egress?
[04:17] Samir: Yes, you'd need SG rules between runtime subnets and the KV backend. Also ensure route tables allow the preferred path, and consider AZ-local replicas to avoid cross-AZ latency.
[04:30] Marta: Encryption — we need TLS and customer-managed KMS for any at-rest model artifacts and logs. Does Redwood support CMKs?
[04:37] Samir: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS for model artifacts and logs. For PrivateLink/control-plane, traffic is TLS and mTLS options are available for the control channel. We'll share the exact cipher and cert rotation docs.
[04:58] Eli: Marta, we can pass our SOC2 pack and KMS integration doc — we'll put it in the shared drive after.
[05:05] Marta: Thanks. Also want to confirm audit logs retention — we may require 12 months.
[05:10] Samir: We can support longer retention as an add-on; we log request IDs, agent IDs, and payload metadata per your compliance needs.
[05:22] Jamal: On quantization: we plan to run 4-bit quant models to reduce memory, but curious if quantization changes KV cache behavior or batching efficiency?
[05:33] Samir: Quant reduces model memory and can reduce per-token compute time, but it doesn't change KV cache semantics. The runtime's attention caches (KV caches) still store float32/float16 depending on model/layout; some quant pipelines compress keys differently. The main impact is memory pressure — with quant you can pack more models per GPU which reduces cross-host calls but increases contention for GPU memory if you're swapping. Batching improves amortized throughput; with quant the compute per token drops, so batching becomes even more efficient cost-wise. However long tail latency for first token (cold start) is unchanged unless you keep workers hot.
[06:12] Priya: Can we pin model workers to specific subnets or AZs? we want to ensure traffic and cache locality.
[06:20] Samir: Yes, in Dedicated/Private you can set placement policies to pin workers to subnets/AZs. We recommend one or two AZs for hot-serving to keep KV cache warm and avoid cross-AZ network hops. Reserve capacity across the region for failover.
[06:39] Noah: Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink: what's recommended?
[06:44] Samir: Transit Gateway is great for multi-VPC large-scale connectivity; it introduces minimal latency if you peer correctly, but cost can be higher. PrivateLink is better when you want to avoid routing across TGW and have a direct endpoint into our control plane — it reduces blast radius and avoids exposing services via IGWs. For data plane high-throughput inference we often recommend VPC peering or TGW with localized routing to avoid extra NAT hops.
[07:10] Priya: NAT egress costs are a concern, our finance team flagged heavy S3 model pulls could be expensive if they go through NAT. Recommended pattern?
[07:18] Samir: Use S3 VPC endpoints (Gateway endpoints) for model artifacts to avoid NAT charges. For model pulls in a private environment, we suggest pre-warming model artifacts in local storage or EBS snapshots attached to nodes, so you avoid repeated S3 pulls at scale.
[07:34] Jamal: Does Redwood support serving from local EBS snapshots in private deployment?
[07:39] Samir: Yes, Private can mount local EBS or NVMe; many customers bake AMIs with model artifacts or use EBS-backed local caches. That reduces startup and model loads during scale-outs.
[07:53] Marta: DNS wise — we run Route53 with Resolver endpoints. Are there DNS requirements?
[07:58] Samir: We support Route53 Resolver endpoints; we recommend using the VPC resolver with conditional forwarding for our control plane hostnames if you're using PrivateLink. Also make sure to avoid split-horizon conflicts — sometimes internal hostnames collide with Redwood hostnames, leading to weird failures.
[08:23] Priya: Any specific port or SG rules we need to open for model-serving?
[08:28] Samir: Mainly TLS port 443 for control plane via PrivateLink. For data plane, ports depend on your chosen transport (HTTP/2 gRPC etc.) — we'll provide a list. Also SG rules for inter-node KV traffic (custom port), and allow traffic between runtime subnets and model storage.
[08:45] Noah: We have a strict requirement to limit public IPs — we'd rather not have any EIPs on runtime hosts. Is that possible?
[08:51] Samir: Yes, you can run fully private nodes without EIPs. For control plane connectivity, use PrivateLink. For egress to AWS services, use VPC endpoints so no NAT is necessary. If you need outbound internet for some telemetry you can funnel through a central egress proxy that we can whitelist.
[09:10] Jamal: Let's dig into KV cache latency numbers — what are realistic p50/p95 for in-process vs networked KV?
[09:18] Samir: In-process KV: p50 sub-ms per cache hit, p95 typically <1ms. Networked Redis-like KV in same AZ: p50 ~1-2ms, p95 3-5ms depending on instance size. Cross-AZ adds another 2-8ms. If your model needs many KV lookups per token, that multiplies. So design workload to favor in-process cache for the hot path.
[09:46] Jamal: For our multi-turn chat (avg 8 tokens per turn) that could add up.
[09:50] Samir: Exactly — if each token needs a KV hit, 5ms per hit at p95 times 8 tokens is 40ms. Combine with model compute and network and you breach SLOs.
[10:05] Priya: What about batching parameters? we run variable-length prompts, how does Redwood do dynamic batching?
[10:12] Samir: Runtime supports workload-aware batching with sequence length histograms. You can set max batch size and max latency window; the engine will batch smaller sequences preferentially. We also have adaptive batching that reacts to observed latency targets. For low-latency workloads keep max latency window small (5-10ms) and lower batch size to avoid tail latency spikes.
[10:38] Noah: Any suggestions on instance types and GPU memory for quant models?
[10:44] Samir: For 4-bit quant models, mid-range GPUs (A10G/A100-40) often fit. If you want more concurrency, A10Gs give good price/perf. For memory-heavy models you might want A100-80 or multiple GPUs with NVLink. Also consider CPU and network: use Enhanced Networking (ENA) for low-latency inter-node traffic.
[11:10] Priya: We plan to do a pilot with 10QPS initially. What should we watch for in terms of scaling behavior?
[11:16] Samir: Watch cold-starts, KV cache warmup, and autoscaler thresholds. Start with warmed workers and a small burst policy to absorb traffic. Monitor token latency distribution and model load. We'll help you define the autoscaling policy (concurrency per worker, warmup count).
[11:38] Jamal: When you say warm workers — do you mean keep a pool of preloaded containers with models?
[11:44] Samir: Exactly. Keep N spare workers per AZ loaded with the model so scale-up is instant. We also support prefetching KV contexts.
[11:52] Marta: For the pilot we'll likely need to sign a Data Processing Addendum and ensure logs don't include PHI.
[11:58] Eli: Understood, we'll route that to legal. We'll also provide redaction options and field-level deny lists.
[12:08] Priya: A couple of nitty gritty on PrivateLink — does it require us to create an interface endpoint in every subnet where we want control plane access?
[12:16] Samir: You create interface endpoints per AZ/subnet you want low-latency control plane. Typically one per AZ in a management subnet is enough. Keep in mind each interface endpoint consumes elastic network interfaces and IPs.
[12:30] Priya: So that circles back to /20 concern. If we spin up endpoints for multiple services we could run out of IPs.
[12:36] Samir: Correct. Use centralized mgmt VPC patterns, shared endpoints, or TGW where appropriate. We can also publish an architecture that uses a small number of endpoints and proxies requests internally.
[12:48] Noah: Is there an obvious recommended architecture diagram for our case (small IP space, 3-AZ prod) ?
[12:55] Samir: Yes, we typically recommend: 1) management VPC with PrivateLink endpoints to Redwood control plane, 2) a serving VPC per environment with peering/TGW to management VPC and cross-AZ placement of runtime nodes, 3) S3 gateway endpoints for model store, 4) Egress via centralized NAT or Egress Proxy depending on policy. We'll send a diagram.
[13:20] Jamal: About TLS termination — where does it happen? on our side or on runtime?
[13:26] Samir: TLS terminates at the runtime load balancer or NLB with TLS pass-through if you want to present your own certs. For Private deployments we can integrate with customer-managed certs and KMS/HSM for key handling.
[13:42] Priya: Any gotchas with Route tables and implicit route propagation we should watch out for?
[13:48] Samir: Watch overlapping routes and ensure your route tables have AZ-local next hops for any intra-AZ traffic. Also check propagation from TGW — sometimes propagation pushes a default route that routes traffic unexpectedly through a TGW instead of local interface endpoints.
[14:05] Marta: For auditability, we'd like all control plane calls to include a correlating request id that maps back to our IAM principals. Is that available?
[14:12] Samir: Yes, we inject request IDs and support passing through your identity (SAML/OIDC) tokens for traceability. We'll document the headers you'll see.
[14:28] Eli: quick interlude — Samir, any empirical numbers you can share from similar customers on end-to-end p95?
[14:33] Samir: For 8k token-ish workloads optimized for latency with in-process KV and same-AZ routing, p50 token latencies of 3-7ms and p95 around 12-25ms are realistic for generation step. End-to-end single-turn (including network and batching) p95 for short prompts in a well-tuned deployment can be 40-90ms. But cross-AZ or networked KV can push p95 above 200ms.
[14:59] Jamal: That's helpful. We will aim for same-AZ and in-process cache for pilot.
[15:06] Priya: Any specific SG/CIDR templates we can reuse?
[15:10] Samir: We'll share a reference repo with security group rules, example subnets (/22 vs /20 guidance), and PrivateLink endpoint provisioning scripts.
[15:22] Noah: On monitoring — what should we expose to our own dashboards?
[15:26] Samir: Expose token latencies, KV hit rates, batch sizes, queue wait times, and GPU utilization. Also expose control plane health and endpoint round-trip times. We can push metrics to Prometheus/Grafana or CloudWatch.
[15:42] Jamal: About quant again — does quantization change the model shard strategy?
[15:47] Samir: Yes slightly. With 4-bit quant you shrink per-shard memory so you can fit more shards per GPU; that reduces cross-GPU communication. But for very large models you still need sharding and NVLink helps. Quant also reduces memory bandwidth, so CPU/GPU pairing may shift.
[16:04] Priya: Are there recommended KC (cache) sizes?
[16:08] Samir: We tune cache sizes based on session length and number of simultaneous sessions. As a rule of thumb allocate enough KV cache memory to hold recent 100-200 tokens per active session; monitor eviction rates. We'll provide a calculator you can run with your expected concurrency.
[16:28] Marta: If we decide to connect via Direct Connect for an on-prem option, latency to Redwood control plane is still a factor?
[16:35] Samir: For on-prem with Direct Connect, you can peer to our private endpoints; the control plane traffic stays on private links. Latency then depends on your DC->AWS link and the chosen region. It's usually better than internet, but you still want AZ-local serving for the hot path if possible.
[16:54] Priya: Are there any specific roles/permissions we need in IAM for the provisioning scripts?
[16:59] Samir: We'll give a least-privilege IAM policy. It includes Create/Describe VPC endpoints, manage route tables, SGs, and read S3/GW endpoints. We can also supply CloudFormation/Terraform modules.
[17:15] Noah: Cost question — PrivateLink endpoints per AZ add charges. For cost-sensitive envs is TGW cheaper?
[17:23] Samir: TGW can be cheaper at scale for lots of VPC interconnects, PrivateLink is cost-effective when you want to limit blast radius and keep control-plane traffic private. We'll model costs based on number of endpoints and expected bandwidth.
[17:38] Jamal: Let's cover a hypothetical failure mode: AZ failure and model state consistency. If an AZ fails, how do we ensure KV cache doesn't cause huge cold-start surge?
[17:48] Samir: Recommended: reserve warm capacity in a secondary AZ (a small warm pool) and use gradual failover. Avoid draining live sessions simultaneously; use sticky routing to preserve session affinity and failover gradually. Also snapshot important KV contexts to a durable store for quick reload.
[18:12] Priya: We're concerned about DNS TTLs causing stale entries post-failover. Any advice?
[18:18] Samir: Keep low TTLs for service endpoints in failover-sensitive flows, and ensure your resolver has conditional forwarding behavior so you can update records quickly. Route53 health checks and failover routing policies help.
[18:33] Marta: For the pilot, what security docs will you send?
[18:38] Eli: We'll share: SOC2 pack, KMS/HSM integration guide, PrivateLink architecture doc, and a sample SOW for the pilot.
[18:47] Samir: Also adding a networking runbook and Terraform module samples.
[18:52] Priya: On the topic of observability payloads — we don't want payload-level logs. Do you allow token-level metrics without payload?
[18:58] Samir: Yes, we can redact payloads and only send telemetry metrics and hashes for quality checks.
[19:06] Jamal: Any notable gotchas with autoscaling on Kubernetes vs bare metal?
[19:12] Samir: Kubernetes autoscalers may cause pod churn that flushes in-process KV caches; if you rely on in-process cache, set appropriate pod disruption budgets and prefer node-level autoscaling with pre-warmed pods. For bare-metal or managed nodepools we recommend keeping a small steady worker count.
[19:34] Priya: Would you recommend node autoscaling at the GPU level only?
[19:38] Samir: Yes, scale at GPU/node level and use internal request queues to smooth spikes. Avoid frequent scale-to-zero for hot workloads.
[19:51] Noah: Can you run a quick demo of a sample route table + endpoint referencing?
[19:56] Samir: (shares screen) here's a route table example: management subnet with PrivateLink ENI, route to local NACLs, security group allowing inbound 443 from serving VPC CIDR, peering route for data plane. Note the explicit route to the PrivateLink interface endpoint.
[20:25] Priya: That helps — we'll need the exact cloudformation.
[20:29] Samir: We'll attach it to the follow-up.
[20:32] Jamal: About model artifact integrity — are there checksums/hashes we can validate?
[20:37] Samir: Yes, we publish artifact SHA256 checks and support signed artifacts in S3. If you use our artifact registry we can enforce immutability.
[20:46] Marta: One more on compliance: will logs show user input? we need to avoid PHI PII leakage.
[20:52] Eli: We have redaction and field-level deny. We'll work with you to define the retention and redaction rules.
[20:59] Priya: If we run the pilot, what's the expected timeline for setting up PrivateLink and endpoints in our account?
[21:05] Samir: Typically 3-7 business days: endpoint creation, route table updates, IAM roles, and test harness. If you pre-share CIDRs and SGs we can do it faster.
[21:18] Noah: Cost again: egress logs to S3 and NAT charges — if we keep everything in VPC S3 endpoints, that removes NAT costs?
[21:25] Samir: Correct, gateway S3 endpoints avoid NAT egress. Also consider lifecycle and compression for logs to limit S3 costs.
[21:36] Jamal: For the pilot, we'd prefer in-process KV + sticky sessions to meet latency targets. Any reason not to do that?
[21:44] Samir: That's a solid choice for latency-sensitive workloads. Just watch for pod churn and affinity. If you anticipate massive horizontal scale, consider hybrid approach with per-AZ shared KV.
[21:58] Priya: Are there sample SLAs for Dedicated/Private?
[22:02] Eli: Yes, we have SLA tiers; we'll attach them. Dedicated has latency and availability targets with credits.
[22:10] Marta: Can we require that the control plane never logs raw inputs?
[22:15] Eli: Yes, we can lock down logging for the control plane and only store metadata. We'll reflect that in the DPA.
[22:26] Samir: returning to a couple final technical notes: enable Enhanced Networking on instances, prefer single-AZ cold-path optimization, use NVMe/EBS for model cache, and pre-warm the KV for expected sessions.
[22:44] Priya: Thanks — that was very concrete.
[22:48] Noah: Next steps recap?
[22:50] Eli: Recap: 1) Samir to send PrivateLink architecture + TF modules + route table examples, 2) Samir/Eli to send SOC2/KMS docs, 3) Aurelius to confirm CIDRs and AZ count, 4) schedule pilot onboarding the week of 2026-12-20.
[23:10] Priya: We'll get CIDR and IP inventory by 2026-12-15.
[23:14] Marta: We'll review SOC2 and KMS needs by 2026-12-12.
[23:18] Jamal: We'll prepare sample prompt/workload so you can model latency.
[23:22] Eli: Great — we'll follow up with the attachments. Anyone have any last minute questions?
[23:28] (brief silence)
[23:32] Priya: All good. Thanks everyone.
[23:34] Eli: Thanks, we'll send follow-up. Bye.

Notes: transcription includes occasional misheard words in-line (k-v cash, Privatelink), speaker interruptions, and natural speech. The transcript timestamps are approximate and intended to reflect cadence across a ~62 minute call.
